h: פָּרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים, מַאֲמָר ד׳ Parshas Shekalim — Maamar Daled

p: And it is brought in the Zohar Chadash,
in the passage beginning "Another explanation: This":
which returned to its place, etc.";
at the root, in the very beginning of Thought;
and this is as we said (Maamarim 1–2),
that through the mitzvah of shekalim
This is what they said in the Yerushalmi
(שְׁקָלִים פֶּרֶק ב׳ הֲלָכָה ג׳ ט, ב)
יִתֵּן כָּל אֶחָד עֲשָׂרָה גֵּרָה וְכוּלֵּי
let each one give ten gerah, etc." —
as they said in the holy Zohar
"Ten utterances in the work of Creation
and ten utterances at Mattan Torah, etc."
And the ten utterances of Creation
are the ten sefiros, as is known.
as they said in the Zohar Chadash.
"The rich shall not give more (Shemos ibid. 15) —
as it is said in Sefer Yetzirah:
And the poor shall not give less (ibid.) —
he shall not diminish from ten,
כְּמָה דְּאַתְּ אָמַר עֶשֶׂר וְלֹא תֵּשַׁע
as it is said: ten and not nine";
Now here the Ra'aya Mehemna explains
as referring to wealth in Torah,
and not to those wealthy in money,
since it is discussing the ten sefiros.
And the matter of "ten and not nine,
that is written in Sefer Yetzirah —
they explained it as referring to the attribute of Da'as,
which is the inner aspect of Kesser.
This is what it says: "and the rich" —
the rich one is rich in knowledge,
"And by knowledge are the chambers filled
with all precious and pleasant wealth."
And one who is rich in Da'as
which alludes to the first three sefiros
and about this it is said:
כְּמָה דְּאַתְּ אָמַר עֶשֶׂר וְלֹא אַחַד עָשָׂר.
as it is said: ten and not eleven."
it is brought (the piyut Echad Mi Yode'a):
that it is unthinkable, chas v'shalom,
that the song is a mere riddle and idle words;
that wherever this number is found,
the reference is to what it specified.
וְאַחַד עָשָׂר כּוֹכָבִים וְגוֹמֵר [בְּרֵאשִׁית לז, ט]
and the intent is the eleven tribes
and there is a count of eleven tribes
that he would rule over them;
and then Yosef too is considered
in the aspect of the sun,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א׳ קעו, ב)
that Yaakov and Yosef are one,
And then the count is eleven tribes.
Likewise we find the number eleven
in the spices of the ketores:
and they correspond to the ten sefiros,
while galbanum has a foul smell,
among the spices of the ketores;
when it is together with them,
and it alludes to the sinners of Yisrael
meaning that they too are destined
to give off a good fragrance,
Among the tribes too we find
"There is none greater than the tribe of Yehudah
וְאֵין לְךָ יָרוּד מִשֵּׁבֶט דָּן וְכוּלֵּי
and none lower than the tribe of Dan, etc."
That is: from the tribe of Yehudah
and of the tribe of Dan it is brought
"The tribe of Dan, which the cloud expelled —
הָיוּ כּוּלָּם עוֹבְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְכוּלֵּי
they were all idol worshippers, etc."
That is, the cloud expelled them
that they have no share in the World to Come,
that they are not included in
כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם וְכוּלֵּי [סַנְהֶדְרִין צ, א]
And they set up the idol of Michah
וְאִיתָא (תַּנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פֶּרֶק כו)
and it is brought (Tanna d'Vei Eliyahu Rabbah, chapter 26):
meaning he rebelled against the very root;
and it listed him before Yeravam,
of whom they said (ibid.), "At 'Lo yihyeh' Yeravam kicked."
right at the Exodus from Egypt,
this is the idol of Michah";
that is, he carried across the silver
from which Michah made the idol.
Michah was the one crushed into the brickwork
and Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom, took him out,
and he rebelled against the root, "Anochi."
Therefore the tribe of Dan is called
And the one rich in Da'as —
with all precious and pleasant wealth" —
"And every precious thing his eye beheld";
and it is brought in the Midrash
"This is Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues:
things that were not revealed to Moshe
were revealed to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues."
That is: Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom,
knew nothing at all of evil,
he was in the secret of Da'as,
in the joining of Chochmah and Binah;
that is, the Torah she'b'al peh
Had it not been for the sin,
his portion in Torah she'b'al peh
for nothing would have been given to them
but the five books of the Torah
who was a son of converts:
and it is from the fiftieth gate,
which is reserved for baalei teshuvah
וְלֹא נִיתַּן לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
and was not given to Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom
for it was not his portion,
since he never knew of evil.
Only, there was revealed to him
would in the future innovate (Vayikra Rabbah 22:1),
but it was not given to him,
for this was the portion of Rabbi Akiva,
who was the root of Torah she'b'al peh.
(This was explained in Chanukah, maamar 2, and elsewhere.)
are likewise called rich in Da'as —
meaning that it is the inner aspect of Kesser.
which alludes to the deeds of the wicked
that the galbanum, which alludes to the sinners of Yisrael,
will also give off a good fragrance,
and there is a remedy even for those
who were considered as having no
share in the World to Come,
since they are of the seed of Yaakov —
even one who rebelled against the root,
That is, it will become clear
that the darkness existed so that there would be
as it says in the holy Zohar
"The Holy One, blessed be He, reveals
And why does He reveal them?
Because He knows what is in the darkness, etc.;
for were it not for the darkness,
the depths and the hidden things.
And the light dwells with Him —
that is revealed from within the darkness, etc."
on his own part knew nothing of evil,
for he was like Adam HaRishon
that none of his be cast away,
and that even the galbanum, alluding to sinners,
should give off a good fragrance.
This is what it says: "The rich shall not give more —
meaning one who is rich in Da'as,
like Yaakov, from the side of the Middle Pillar,
and who has attained all precious and pleasant wealth,
that he would count the deep and hidden on its own,
that is, he would count Kesser Elyon
and also the attribute of Da'as.
for in truth it is all one
וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ לֹא יַרְבֶּה עַל עֶשֶׂר
This is what they said: "He shall not exceed ten" —
for in truth, when the galbanum is refined,
is one with the greatest of the tribes;
meaning, it is not part of evil at all,
so that there would be "very good,"
for there is no good except that
as they said in the holy Zohar (there).
is the inner aspect of Kesser,
namely the part graspable by man
And likewise it is all one:
the deep, the hidden, and the darkness,
which alludes to the first utterance,
in which there is no grasp whatsoever.
this is the light that is revealed
and this is "ten and not eleven."
meaning a tzaddik who conquers his inclination
which is reserved for baalei teshuvah.
that there are only nine sefiros
for the creation of the world,
since the attribute of Kesser Elyon
and is hidden from all thought;
and he would say that it is not counted
"And the poor shall not diminish from ten,
כְּמָה דְּאַתְּ אָמַר עֶשֶׂר וְלֹא תֵּשַׁע
as it is said: ten and not nine" —
that there is a hidden intellect
that there be returned to them
as they said in the Zohar Chadash.
A crown denotes a crown of kingship;
over whom then does one reign and rule?
he is in the aspect of a king
This is why Hashem Yisbarach paired,
in the making of the Mishkan,
with the lowest of the tribes,
because the small and the great
while in Divrei HaYamim (II 2:13) it is written,
"the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan" —
for his father was from Naftali
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא כִּי תִשָּׂא יג)
(as stated in Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Sisa 13).
Likewise in the future there will join with Mashiach
one from the tribe of Dan,
(כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק ג׳ קצד, ב)
That is, the great and the small
וְכָל אֶחָד יֵשׁ לוֹ דָּבָר אֶחָד
and each one has one thing
in which he is crowned with a crown
On Shabbos, Moshe Rabbeinu, alav hashalom,
the crowns of Mattan Torah to Yisrael,
as we said from the Pri Etz Chaim;
for the crowns to be returned to Yisrael
when they give the shekalim, even on a weekday,
as we said and explained above (maamar 2).

paragraphs.text: Exodus 30:13-15 — “This they shall give, everyone who passes among those counted: half a shekel by the sacred shekel; the shekel is twenty gerah. Half a shekel is an offering to Hashem. ... The rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel when giving Hashem's offering to atone for your lives.” The first and third verses are quoted here, with the intervening verse omitted. Rav Tzadok develops the ten gerah of the half-shekel and the equal obligation of rich and poor.

paragraphs.text: Zohar Chadash, Ki Sisa, beginning Davar acher zeh yitnu — “Another interpretation of This they shall give: How carefully people must guard their ways! When that righteous one was sold, all ten levels shut off their lights, for the illumination of the Ancient One flows for the benefit of the earth only through him. ... Therefore the ten gerah that restore him to his place are a ransom for the soul. They shine upon the place called soul from the place called Israel; heaven shines upon this earth and gives her all her adornments, so that she may be joined above.” The passage connects the sale of the righteous one with the darkening of the ten levels and their repair through the ten gerah. The exact digital paragraph is verified; the manuscript's printed folio 45b has not independently been checked against a scan.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Vayikra, discourse 25 — “Ten, ten: why does it say this? Ten for the work of Creation, and ten for the giving of the Torah: ten utterances in the work of Creation and ten utterances at the giving of the Torah. What is this about? The world was created only for the Torah. Whenever Israel occupies itself with Torah, the world endures.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Yitzchak on Sefer Yetzirah 1:4 — “‘Ten and not nine’: not to exclude Kesser, though called Ayin; ‘ten and not eleven’: Da'as is not counted, for it is not a sefirah of its own but the union of Chochmah and Binah.” R. paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 2 — “Every person who possesses daas is as though the Temple were built in his days. The Temple is the place specially set aside for the Divine Presence to dwell. One who possesses daas has attained the quality of daas, which is the inwardness of keser, as is known; this is apprehended through the holy spirit. Then his heart becomes a dwelling for the Divine Presence and is called My holy mountain, and it is as though the Temple were built in his days.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The same identification of daas as the inwardness of keser explains why spiritual wealth is more than accumulated information: it makes the heart a place for the Divine Presence, even when the physical Temple is absent. This clarifies the inward restoration associated here with the ten gerah.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 41a — “Abaye said: We have received the tradition that there is no poverty except in understanding. In the West they say: One who has this has everything; one who lacks this, what does he have? If he has acquired this, what does he lack? If he has not acquired this, what has he acquired?” The Aramaic this refers to daas. Rav Tzadok uses the saying to distinguish wealth in understanding from wealth in money.

paragraphs.text: Pesach Haggadah, Echad Mi Yodea, eleven stanza — “Who knows eleven? I know eleven: eleven stars, ten commandments, nine months of birth, eight days of circumcision, seven days of the week, six orders of Mishnah, five books of Torah, four mothers, three fathers, two tablets of the covenant; One is our God, in heaven and on earth.” The cumulative song explicitly identifies eleven with stars and twelve with the tribes. Rav Tzadok interprets its numerical correspondences through Yosef’s dream.

paragraphs.text: Genesis 37:9 — “He dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers, saying: I have dreamed another dream; behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.” The eleven stars are the dream's eleven brothers; Yosef stands outside that count. Rav Tzadok connects this with Yosef's particular unity with Yaakov.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Derashos HaRan, Derush 1 — “A deficiency in one part can bring the perfections of the other parts from potential to actual. This is hinted in the galbanum: though unfit itself, it can arouse the qualities of the other spices.” The Ran explains how the galbanum adds to the whole: it brings out the fragrance of the others, as Rav Tzadok goes on to say evil exists so that there will be “very good.”

paragraphs.text: Keritot 6b — “Rav Chana bar Bizna said in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida: Any fast that does not include some of the transgressors of Israel is not a fast, for galbanum has a foul smell, yet Scripture counted it among the ingredients of the incense.” The source requires the inclusion of sinners in the communal fast, just as galbanum belongs in the incense mixture. Rav Tzadok develops its inclusion into the eventual transformation of the evil smell itself.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 21b — “The good figs are the completely righteous; the bad figs are the completely wicked. Lest you say their hope is lost and their prospect has ceased, Scripture says: The mandrakes have given fragrance; both these and those are destined to give fragrance.” The Gemara explicitly preserves hope for those described as completely wicked. Rav Tzadok applies that future fragrance to the galbanum and to the lowest tribe.

paragraphs.text: Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 10 — “The Sages say: The tribe of Dan, which the cloud expelled, were all worshippers of idols, as it is said: You were weary and exhausted, and did not fear God.” This is one of the Midrash's explanations of those left behind whom Amalek attacked. Rav Tzadok cites it to establish the severity of Dan's condition before arguing that even this lowliness is ultimately repairable.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 90a — “All Israel has a share in the World to Come, as it is said: Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which to glory. These are the ones who have no share in the World to Come: one who says that resurrection of the dead is not taught in the Torah, that Torah is not from Heaven, and an apostate.” The Mishnah states both the general promise and specified exclusions. Rav Tzadok's subsequent discussion concerns the ultimate repair of those whom the cited sources treat as excluded; it does not erase the Mishnah's distinctions.

paragraphs.text: Judges 18:30-31 — “The children of Dan set up the carved image for themselves. Yonasan son of Gershom, son of Menasheh, and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day the land went into exile. They established for themselves the carved image that Michah had made, throughout the time the house of God was in Shiloh.” The biblical account explicitly joins the tribe of Dan to Michah's image and places its worship alongside the sanctuary at Shiloh.

paragraphs.text: Tanna Debei Eliyahu Rabbah 26 — “I am Hashem your God teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, looked through the entire world, from its beginning to its end, and foresaw ten people who rebelled against Him. ... Against I am Hashem your God, Michah rebelled; against You shall have no other gods, Yeravam rebelled.” The chapter arranges ten rebels against the Ten Commandments. Rav Tzadok focuses on Michah's position at the root represented by the first commandment.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 103b — “And trouble shall pass through the sea: Rabbi Yochanan said, This is the idol of Michah. It was taught: Rabbi Nasan says, From Garev to Shiloh is three mil, and the smoke of the altar and the smoke of Michah's idol would mingle with one another.” Rav Tzadok understands the passage through the sea as the carrying of the silver later used for Michah's idol. The identification of the carried substance as silver is his explanatory reading, not an explicit statement in these words of the Gemara.

paragraphs.text: Rashi, Sanhedrin 101b, s.v. Nismachmech babinyan — “He was crushed into the building: in Egypt they put him into the building in place of a brick. As explained in the aggadah, Moshe said to the Holy One, blessed be He: You have harmed this people, for now, if they lack bricks, they place Israel's children in the building. He told him: They are destroying thorns, for it is revealed before Me that if these children lived they would be utterly wicked. If you wish, test it and take one of them out. He went and took out Michah.” Rashi records this as his first explanation and then offers another: Michah became impoverished through work in building. Rav Tzadok follows the first explanation.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 22b — “Rav Adda son of Rabbi Chanina said: Had Israel not sinned, they would have been given only the five books of the Torah and the book of Yehoshua, because it describes the division of the Land of Israel. paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 2:3 — “We find everywhere ‘a law to Moses from Sinai.’ Since it says ‘from Sinai,’ why was it not written? We have said that this is Moses’ Oral Torah, which the blessed God illuminated in Moses’ understanding and which he innovated through his dialectical reasoning.... It is called ‘a law to Moses from Sinai’ because Moses knew explicitly that these teachings were from Sinai, like the entire Written Torah; he transmitted them to Israel as laws without their reasons.... This is what was said of Rabbi Akiva in Menachos 29b: his pupils asked him, ‘Rabbi, from where do you derive this?’ He answered them, ‘It is a law given to Moses at Sinai.’ Although the Midrash says, ‘Every precious thing his eye has seen’—this refers to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues; things that were not revealed to Moses were revealed to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues—and the Gemara likewise says that Moses sat at the end of eight rows and did not understand what they were saying, Rabbi Akiva nevertheless did not attain the reason for the law given to Moses at Sinai: that was Moses our teacher’s portion. Thus the Gemara says that Moses’ mind was set at rest. From this he saw that his own understanding was higher, and that his portion in the Oral Torah had been attained by no other person. The portion of Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues in the Oral Torah did not belong to Moses, because he had never caused corruption. He did not need the increase of wisdom—the fiftieth gate entrusted to the penitent to repair the increase of vexation.” This is the exact self-reference named here. Rav Tzaddik distinguishes Moses’ uniquely understood Sinaitic oral teaching from Rabbi Akiva’s restorative Oral Torah, associated with the fiftieth gate and repentance.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 2:5 — “From the beginning of the creation of the world, the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw the deeds of the righteous and the deeds of the wicked. ‘The earth was unformed and void’ — these are the deeds of the wicked. ‘God said: Let there be light’ — these are the deeds of the righteous. But I do not know which He desires. Since it is written, ‘God saw the light, that it was good,’ He desires the deeds of the righteous and does not desire the deeds of the wicked.” The Midrash itself explicitly distinguishes God’s desire for good deeds from His foreknowledge of evil deeds. Rav Tzadok’s discussion of the eventual good that emerges from darkness should be read with that distinction intact.

paragraphs.text: Ecclesiastes 10:1 — “Dead flies make the perfumer's oil give off a foul odor; a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.” In its plain meaning, a little folly can spoil or outweigh wisdom. Rav Tzadok develops a mystical reading of preciousness beyond wisdom and honor; that exposition should not be mistaken for the verse's straightforward warning.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 104b — “The interpreters of scriptural allusions would say: They all come to the World to Come, as it is said: Gilead is Mine, Menasheh is Mine, Ephraim is the stronghold of My head, Yehudah is My lawgiver. ... Gilead refers to Achav, who fell at Ramas Gilead; Menasheh is understood literally; Ephraim, the stronghold of My head, refers to Yeravam, who came from Ephraim.” This aggadic interpretation supplies the restorative reading Rav Tzadok invokes. It should be distinguished from the Mishnah's earlier list of those denied a share.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Tetzaveh, discourse 18 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, reveals deep and concealed things; He reveals all the hidden supernal depths. Why does He reveal them? Because He knows what is in darkness. Were it not for darkness, light would not be known. ... Were it not for darkness, deep and concealed things would not be revealed. And light dwells with Him: what light is this? The light that is revealed from within darkness.” The precise Aramaic wording is verified in the original Zohar text. It explains the manifestation of light through what concealed it; the manuscript's adjacent printed-folio references require independent scan collation.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah 17 — “Dan was joined with the greatest tribe, for then there was a revelation like the future, when the circles will be revealed … for in a circle the end joins the head.” Chanukah 17 explains why the Mishkan and the Mikdash were built by the greatest and the lowest tribes: they revealed the future circle (Taanis 31a), where the lowest touches the highest, as Dan will again stand with Mashiach.

paragraphs.text: Tanchuma, Ki Sisa 13 — “There is no tribe greater than Yehudah, and none lower than Dan, which descended from the maidservants. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: Let him come and be joined to him, so that he should not grow arrogant, for great and small are equal before the Holy One, blessed be He. ... The Mishkan was made by these two tribes, and the Temple likewise: Shlomo from Yehudah and Chiram from Dan. ... His father was from Naftali and his mother from Dan.” The Midrash reads the different tribal descriptions in Kings and Chronicles together. Rav Tzadok uses the partnership to show the equal necessity of the greatest and the lowest contribution.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Balak, discourse 13 — “And its rider will fall backward: this is Serayah, who is destined to come with the Messiah of Ephraim. He will be from the tribe of Dan and will execute vengeance and wage wars against the other nations. When he arises, one then awaits Israel's redemption, as it is written: For Your salvation I have hoped, Hashem.” The Zohar explicitly identifies Serayah's companion as the Messiah of Ephraim. Rav Tzadok's wording here refers generally to the messianic partnership of the tribe of Dan.
